@@ -0,0 +1,104 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-07",
+	"title": "The soldier and the owl, a mast in front, and the seven pairs",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "thaaw-thahaan",
+			"heading": "thaaw thá-hǎan, a soldier on the bridge",
+			"body": [
+				"ท has a head that curls in, a back that climbs straight up, and an arch that marches back down — a soldier pacing the harbor bridge.",
+				"Harbor again: ท is low class, like ค last lesson. The sound is th, a t carried out on a breath, so ทาง (thaang), a way or a direction, puffs where an English t would not.",
+				"Watch it in final position instead and the breath disappears: บาท (bàat) is the baht, and the ท there is a plain t-stop. That is the dead-ending rule from lesson three, unchanged."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "haaw-nok-huuk",
+			"heading": "haaw nók-hûuk, an owl on the water",
+			"body": [
+				"ฮ is a single round eye with a zigzag crest over it — an owl's ear-tufts, blinking at the night harbor.",
+				"It says h, and ฮา (haa) is to laugh. It is the rarest letter you will meet in this course: barely one character in ten thousand of running Thai.",
+				"Learn it anyway, and learn it now. It is the last piece of a pattern that covers seven sounds, and without it the pattern has a hole in exactly the place a beginner most needs it."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "cousin-pairs",
+			"heading": "Seven sounds, two letters each",
+			"body": [
+				"Every letter below breathes or hisses — none of them can be hummed, and none of them is a plain stop. That is the one group where class is not derivable from the sound, and Thai gives each of those sounds two letters: one at the harbor, one at the temple.",
+				"ค is harbor and ข is temple. Both say kh.",
+				"ช is harbor and ฉ is temple. Both say ch.",
+				"ท is harbor and ถ is temple. Both say th.",
+				"พ is harbor and ผ is temple. Both say ph, and the two are the same figure with the head turned the other way.",
+				"ฟ is harbor and ฝ is temple. Both say f, and they differ by the same head turn.",
+				"ซ is harbor and ส is temple. Both say s.",
+				"ฮ is harbor and ห is temple. Both say h.",
+				"Seven rows, not fourteen letters. You already hold the whole harbor column; the temple column arrives one lesson at a time, and each one you meet is a letter whose sound you can already make."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "why-two",
+			"prompt": "The two letters in a row sound identical. Say what the second one is for, and what you would lose if Thai had only one of them.",
+			"revealSlideId": "why-two-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "why-two-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "why-two",
+			"answers": [
+				"The district is the difference: one is low class, the other high class, and class is half of every tone decision.",
+				"With one letter per sound, those syllables could only carry the tones the low class can reach. The second letter is how Thai writes the other tones for the same sound."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "mast-vowels",
+			"heading": "เ and เ-ะ, the mast raised in front",
+			"body": [
+				"เ is a single mast written before its consonant and sounded after it. Reading order and writing order come apart here for the first time: เท is read thee, not ee-th.",
+				"Held long it is ee, the vowel of a level gaze. เท (thee) is to pour.",
+				"เ-ะ is the same mast with two stacked hooks behind it — the short, clipped version of the same vowel. It is rarely written out in full, and the next slide is why."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "e-with-a-final",
+			"heading": "What the hooks turn into",
+			"body": [
+				"The stacked hooks of เ-ะ only survive when nothing follows. Add a final consonant and they collapse into a small ็ perched over it.",
+				"เด็ก (dèk) is a child. เย็น (yen) is cool or evening. เก็บ (gèp) is to keep or put away.",
+				"ก็ (gâaw) is the odd one out and worth knowing on sight: a bare ก wearing the same roof, meaning then or also, and one of the commonest words in the language.",
+				"This is the second vowel you have met that is written differently depending on what follows it. ะ was the first, back in lesson four, when it became a curl over the consonant."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "hooks-or-roof",
+			"prompt": "You want to write the short e sound twice — once in a syllable ending in k, once in a syllable ending in nothing. What changes between them?",
+			"revealSlideId": "hooks-or-roof-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "hooks-or-roof-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "hooks-or-roof",
+			"answers": [
+				"With a final consonant the hooks become the ็ roof: เด็ก.",
+				"With nothing following, the hooks stay written out after the consonant.",
+				"The sound does not change at all. Only the spelling reacts to what comes next."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "more-words",
+			"heading": "Words you can read now",
+			"body": [
+				"ทุก (thúk) is every. ทันที (than thii) is at once. นาที (naa-thii) is a minute, and บางที (baang thii) is perhaps.",
+				"ทาน (thaan) is to eat. ทีม (thiim) is a team and เกม (geem) is a game — both borrowed, both spelled exactly as they sound.",
+				"บทบาท (bòt bàat) is a role. ทับ (tháp) is to lie on top of something."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,88 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-08",
+	"title": "The boat and the monkey, twin masts, and two letters that land as n",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "raaw-ruuea",
+			"heading": "raaw ruuea, a boat flying its flag",
+			"body": [
+				"ร sits with its head low at the waterline and a pennant line flying up and hooking over to the right — a boat's prow with a flag on it.",
+				"Harbor, so low class. At the front of a syllable it is a rolled r, the outboard motor turning over: รัก (rák) is love, รับ (ráp) is to receive.",
+				"Thai speakers roll it hard in careful speech and barely at all in fast speech. Both are normal. What matters for reading is that it is there."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "laaw-ling",
+			"heading": "laaw ling, a monkey on a post",
+			"body": [
+				"ล has its head at the base and one long tail arching right over its back — a monkey crouched on a harbor post.",
+				"Harbor again, low class, and the sound is l lapped off the tongue ridge. ลูก (lûuk) is a child or a piece of fruit. ลม (lom) is wind.",
+				"ล and ร look nothing alike at the front of a word and behave identically at the end of one, which is the next slide."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "landing-as-n",
+			"heading": "Both of them land as n",
+			"body": [
+				"At the tail of a syllable neither letter keeps its own sound. Both flatten into n.",
+				"การ (gaan) is the commonest word built this way: written with ร in last position, pronounced with n. It turns up inside longer words unchanged — รายการ (raai-gaan), a programme or a list, and ทางการ (thaang gaan), official.",
+				"This is not an exception you memorise per word. It is what ร and ล always do in final position, and it is why lesson two's live-endings rule names five letters without naming either of these: they are not a new ending, they are น arriving in disguise."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "final-r",
+			"prompt": "A syllable is written with ร in last position. What sound ends it, and is the syllable live or dead?",
+			"revealSlideId": "final-r-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "final-r-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "final-r",
+			"answers": [
+				"It ends in n.",
+				"Live. น is one of the five endings that keep a syllable live, and ร landing as น inherits that — so การ is a live syllable and takes the live tone rule for its class."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "ae-vowels",
+			"heading": "แ and แ-ะ, two masts instead of one",
+			"body": [
+				"แ is the mast of lesson seven raised twice, side by side, and written in front of its consonant in the same way. The sound is a long flat ae, the vowel in the English word cat, stretched.",
+				"แดง (daaeng) is red. แพง (phaaeng) is expensive. แทน (thaaen) is instead of.",
+				"แ-ะ is the short one: twin masts with the stacked hooks after. It behaves exactly like เ-ะ did last lesson — add a final consonant and the hooks become the ็ roof.",
+				"แยก (yâaek) is to separate or a junction, and it is worth saying out loud beside แรก (râaek), first. One vowel, two words, no overlap in meaning at all."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "one-mast-two",
+			"prompt": "You know one mast and two masts. Say which sound each carries, and what both of them do to reading order.",
+			"revealSlideId": "one-mast-two-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "one-mast-two-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "one-mast-two",
+			"answers": [
+				"One mast, เ, is ee. Two masts, แ, is ae.",
+				"Each one is put down ahead of its consonant and voiced after it. The eye takes them first; the mouth takes them second."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "more-words",
+			"heading": "Words you can read now",
+			"body": [
+				"และ (láe) is and, ละ (lá) is each, and ระดับ (rá dàp) is a level or grade.",
+				"ราคา (raa-khaa) is a price. ดูแล (duu laae) is to look after. ทะเล (thá lee) is the sea.",
+				"เล็ก (lék) is small and เร็ว (reo) is fast — both wearing the ็ roof from last lesson.",
+				"ลึก (lúek) is deep, รีบ (rîip) is to hurry, and รัก (rák) you already have. That is four of the twenty commonest verbs in the language, all readable with what you now hold."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+{

+	"title": "Three letters from the market, and a mast that leans",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",

+			"heading": "A plate, a turtle and a fish",
+			"body": [
+				"จ, jaaw jaan, is a hook curving up and over from a head at mid height — a plate spun on one finger at a noodle stall. The sound is j with no puff behind it, halfway toward the ch of ช.",
+				"ต, dtaaw dtào, is ด with a notch cut into the rim — the dent in the shell where the turtle pulled its head in. The sound is dt: press d and t into one flat sound and let no breath out.",
+				"ป, bpaaw bplaa, is บ with the right wall grown up past the rim — a fish clearing the market basket. The sound is bp, b and p pressed flat together.",
+				"All three stand in the market. Mid class, every one of them, and that is the whole point of teaching them together."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "why-the-market",
+			"heading": "Why the market is the easy district",
+			"body": [
+				"Listen to what จ ต ป have in common with ก ด บ from lesson three: every one of them stops, and none of them releases breath. Hold a hand up and say ปี (bpii), a year. Nothing lands on it.",
+				"That is the market's rule, and it has no exceptions. A Thai consonant that stops and releases no breath is mid class. You do not memorise the list; you listen for the missing puff.",
+				"Compare พ from lesson five, which stops and does breathe, and ม which does not stop at all. Three behaviours, three districts."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "market-or-not",
+			"prompt": "Someone hands you a Thai letter you have never seen and tells you it is pronounced dt. Which district is it in, and how sure can you be?",
+			"revealSlideId": "market-or-not-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "market-or-not-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "market-or-not",
+			"answers": [
+				"The market. Mid class.",
+				"Completely sure, without seeing the letter. A plain unaspirated stop is mid class with no exceptions, so the sound alone settles it."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "o-vowels",
+			"heading": "โ and โ-ะ, the leaning mast",
+			"body": [
+				"โ is a mast whose tip loops once and leans forward over the letter. It is written in front like เ and แ, and it is a long round oo with the mouth in a full circle.",
+				"โต (dtoo) is to grow or to be large. โลก (lôok) is the world. โดย (dooi) is by or by means of.",
+				"โ-ะ is the short one, written with the loop in front and the stacked hooks after — and it is the vowel you have already been reading without knowing it."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-vowel-you-cannot-see",
+			"heading": "The short o that is written with nothing",
+			"body": [
+				"Put a final consonant after โ-ะ and the spelling does not shrink to a roof the way เ-ะ and แ-ะ do. It disappears completely.",
+				"คน (khon) from lesson six is exactly this: ค, nothing, น, and the nothing is a short o. So is ตก (dtòk), to fall, and จน (jon), until.",
+				"That is not a quirk of three words. Two bare consonants side by side with no vowel written between them are read with this vowel, every time, and the full rule — including what happens with three consonants — has a lesson to itself.",
+				"Say it as one syllable. คน is khon in a single beat, never kho-no."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "nothing-between",
+			"prompt": "You meet a two-letter word with no vowel written anywhere in it. What do you put between the letters, and how many syllables is it?",
+			"revealSlideId": "nothing-between-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "nothing-between-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "nothing-between",
+			"answers": [
+				"The short o of โ-ะ, unwritten.",
+				"One syllable. The first letter is the initial, the second is the final, and the vowel between them is never spelled out."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "more-words",
+			"heading": "Words you can read now",
+			"body": [
+				"จะ (jà) marks the future and is the third commonest word in Thai. จาก (jàak) is from. ตาม (dtaam) is to follow or according to.",
+				"เป็น (bpen) is to be — the mast, the roof and a market letter, all three of this course's last two lessons in one very common word.",
+				"ตา (dtaa) is an eye, ตี (dtii) is to hit, ปาก (bpàak) is a mouth, and จับ (jàp) is to catch.",
+				"Some of these end dead — จาก, ปาก, จับ, ตก — and you cannot yet say what tone they take. Mid class on a dead syllable is the one rule of the four still missing, and it arrives in lesson eleven."
+			]

+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-10",
+	"title": "Three ways of saying a short vowel that counts as long",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "ao-and-ai",
+			"heading": "เ-า, ไ and ใ",
+			"body": [
+				"เ-า brackets its consonant: the mast in front, the า post behind. The sound is ao, the yelp in the English how. เอา (ao) is to take or to want. เรา (rao) is we.",
+				"ไ is a mast whose top breaks into a zigzag, written in front and sounded after. The sound is ai, the English word I. ไป (bpai) is to go and ไฟ (fai) is fire.",
+				"ใ is the same sound with the top rolled into a curl instead. ใน (nai) is in, ใจ (jai) is the heart or mind, ใบ (bai) is a leaf.",
+				"ไ and ใ are not two sounds. They are two spellings of one sound, and which one a word uses is a fact about that word."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "which-ai",
+			"heading": "Which ai a word takes",
+			"body": [
+				"ใ is the rare one. It is used in a closed list of about twenty common words and nowhere else; every other ai in the language is written ไ.",
+				"ใน, ใจ, ใบ and ใด (dai, meaning any) are four of them, and ใคร (khrai, who) is a fifth. You will meet the rest as words, not as a rule.",
+				"So the default is ไ. When you see the curled top instead, you are looking at one of the twenty, and the word itself is the thing to remember."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "two-spellings",
+			"prompt": "You hear a Thai word pronounced bpai and have to write it. Which of the two ai spellings do you reach for, and how confident should you be?",
+			"revealSlideId": "two-spellings-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "two-spellings-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "two-spellings",
+			"answers": [
+				"ไ, the zigzag. ไป.",
+				"Very confident. ใ is a closed list of roughly twenty words; anything not on that list takes ไ."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "ao-ai-tone-exception",
+			"ruleId": "ao-ai-tone-exception"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "short-but-live",
+			"heading": "Short in the mouth, long for the tone",
+			"body": [
+				"Say เอา and ไป. Both are over quickly — as short as the ะ of lesson four.",
+				"For tone they are counted the other way. เ-า, ไ and ใ make live syllables, and they take the live rule for their consonant's class, not the dead-short one.",
+				"ไป opens on ป, a market letter, so it takes mid class live: bpai, level. Say it beside ตก from last lesson, which is mid class dead and drops low. Same district, opposite endings, and the vowel is what decides which."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "short-or-live",
+			"prompt": "ไป is over as fast as a short vowel. Why does it not take the dead-syllable rule?",
+			"revealSlideId": "short-or-live-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "short-or-live-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "short-or-live",
+			"answers": [
+				"Because เ-า, ไ and ใ are counted live for tone regardless of how short they sound.",
+				"The syllable ends on the vowel with nothing stopping it, so there is nothing to make it dead. Length of time is not what the rule measures."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "mai-yamok",
+			"ruleId": "mai-yamok"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-repeat-mark",
+			"heading": "ๆ, the mark that means say it twice",
+			"body": [
+				"ๆ is not a letter and has no sound of its own. It stands after a word and tells you to repeat the word.",
+				"เด็ก ๆ is children — เด็ก said twice. ใคร ๆ is anyone at all. A space is normally left in front of the mark.",
+				"Doubling in Thai usually softens or generalises rather than intensifying: the repeated form is vaguer than the single one, not stronger."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "consonant-clusters",
+			"ruleId": "consonant-clusters"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "clusters-named",
+			"heading": "Two consonants, one sound — named here, taught later",
+			"body": [
+				"ใคร has ค and ร back to back with no vowel between them, and it is one syllable, not two: khrai. The two letters run together into a single onset.",
+				"Only three letters ever do this in second position, and the rule slide above names them. That is the whole inventory, and it is closed.",
+				"It is also only half the story. Some pairs that look like clusters are not, one of them is read as a completely different sound, and one of the three letters can be written and not pronounced at all. All of that belongs together in one place, and that place is the clusters lesson.",
+				"Until then: two consonants with nothing between them are either a cluster or an unwritten vowel, and last lesson gave you the other one."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "more-words",
+			"heading": "Words you can read now",
+			"body": [
+				"ใน (nai) is in, and it is one of the commonest words in the language. ไป (bpai) is to go. เรา (rao) is we or us.",
+				"ดีใจ (dii jai) is glad — literally a good heart. ตกใจ (dtòk jai) is startled — a heart that falls.",
+				"ไทย (thai) is Thai. Its consonants have been readable since lesson seven; today's zigzag mast is the last piece it needed."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-11",
+	"title": "The empty basin, which is silent until it is a vowel",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "aaw-aang",
+			"heading": "aaw àang, an empty basin",
+			"body": [
+				"อ is a plain ring standing open — a basin set down among the market stalls, and the market is the class: อ is mid.",
+				"You have already been reading it. Since lesson six it has been the prop under a bare ื, in มือ and คือ, and nothing was asked of it there.",
+				"It has two jobs, and which one it is doing depends only on where it sits in the syllable."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "o-ang-dual-role",
+			"ruleId": "o-ang-dual-role"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "job-one",
+			"heading": "Job one — minding the stall",
+			"body": [
+				"Thai syllables are written consonant first. A word whose first sound is a vowel has no consonant to write, so อ stands in the slot and says nothing.",
+				"อีก (ìik) is more or again. อัน (an) is the classifier for small things. อา (aa) is a parent's younger sibling. อาจ (àat) is may or might.",
+				"In every one of those the ring is silent. It is holding the place, exactly as it held the place under ื."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "job-two",
+			"heading": "Job two — being the vowel aaw",
+			"body": [
+				"Put อ after a consonant with no vowel written, and it stops being silent and becomes a long aaw — a yawn with the jaw dropped all the way.",
+				"พอ (phaaw) is enough. รอ (raaw) is to wait. ตอน (dtaawn) is a part or a moment. นอน (naawn) is to sleep. มอง (maawng) is to look at.",
+				"Two jobs, one glyph, and the position settles it every time: in front of the vowel slot it is a silent consonant, in the vowel slot it is aaw."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-job",
+			"prompt": "Two syllables, each written with อ. In one the ring is the first character; in the other it follows a consonant with nothing between. Which is silent, and which is a vowel?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-job-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-job-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-job",
+			"answers": [
+				"First character: silent. It is minding an empty consonant slot for a word that opens on a vowel.",
+				"After a consonant with nothing between: the vowel aaw.",
+				"You never have to guess. The position is the rule."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "short-aw",
+			"heading": "เ-าะ, the clipped yawn",
+			"body": [
+				"เ-าะ is the short version of the same sound: the mast in front, then the า post and the stacked hooks — three pieces wrapping one very short syllable.",
+				"เกาะ (gàw) is an island, and it is dead-short: the vowel is clipped and nothing follows it.",
+				"Beside it, ออก (àawk) is long. Same aw, held, and then stopped by ก. The two lengths are different vowels in Thai, not a matter of emphasis."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "mid-dead-short",
+			"ruleId": "mid-dead-short"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "mid-dead-long",
+			"ruleId": "mid-dead-long"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-grid-closes",
+			"heading": "The market's four corners",
+			"body": [
+				"Mid class live you have had since lesson three: ตาม (dtaam) sits level.",
+				"Mid class dead is one tone whichever length the vowel is, and that tone is low. เกาะ (gàw) is dead-short and low. ออก (àawk) is dead-long and low. จาก (jàak), ปาก (bpàak) and ตก (dtòk) are all the same corner.",
+				"That closes the market's tone grid. Every syllable opening on ก ด บ จ ต ป or อ now has a tone you can work out from the page alone, live or dead, long or short.",
+				"Compare the low class, which needed two dead rules because the lengths disagree — short goes high, long falls. The market is the simpler district in every direction."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "close-the-grid",
+			"prompt": "บอก and เกาะ both open on a market letter and both end dead, one long and one short. What tone does each take, and how many rules did you need?",
+			"revealSlideId": "close-the-grid-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "close-the-grid-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "close-the-grid",
+			"answers": [
+				"Both are low.",
+				"One rule, effectively. A market letter on a dead syllable gives low, and vowel length makes no difference to it — which is exactly what the harbor does not do."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "more-words",
+			"heading": "Words you can read now",
+			"body": [
+				"ชอบ (châawp) is to like, บอก (bàawk) is to tell, ตอบ (dtàawp) is to answer, and ยอม (yaawm) is to consent.",
+				"ออก (àawk) is to go out, and you will see it on every exit sign in the country.",
+				"อาชีพ (aa chîip) is an occupation. อายุ (aa yú) is age — the word Thai uses where English says how old someone is.",
+				"Eleven lessons in: seven of the nine market letters, the whole harbor side of the seven pairs, and twenty vowel spellings."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,98 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-12",
+	"title": "The temple cousins",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "seven-at-once",
+			"heading": "Seven letters, one move",
+			"body": [
+				"Every letter on this page writes a sound you can already read. What changes is the district: each one takes a sound the harbor owns and gives it to the temple.",
+				"ข is temple kh — cousin of harbor ค. ฉ is temple ch — cousin of ช. ถ is temple th — cousin of ท. ผ is temple ph — cousin of พ. ฝ is temple f — cousin of ฟ. ส is temple s — cousin of ซ. ห is temple h — cousin of ฮ.",
+				"Nothing new arrives at your ear. Everything new arrives at the tone, because tone is decided by district."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "why-the-doubles-exist",
+			"heading": "Why Thai writes one sound twice",
+			"body": [
+				"A harbor letter starting a syllable can never make that syllable rise. A temple letter does it as its default. The doubling is not waste — it is how the script reaches tones one district alone could not.",
+				"So a word spelled with ข and a word spelled with ค can differ by tone alone, and the letter choice is what tells you which you are hearing."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "high-live-rule",
+			"ruleId": "high-live"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "rising-everywhere",
+			"heading": "The temple's home tone, in real words",
+			"body": [
+				"A temple letter opening a live syllable gives a rising tone, and the commonest words in the language demonstrate it over and over.",
+				"ฉัน (chǎn) is I. ผม (phǒm) is I for a man. ของ (khǎawng) is of, or a thing. ถึง (thǔeng) is to reach. หา (hǎa) is to look for. ขอ (khǎaw) is to ask for.",
+				"Say any two of them in a row and you can feel the shape: each one climbs."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "telling-cousins-apart",
+			"heading": "Keeping each pair apart on the page",
+			"body": [
+				"ข and ค share a body; the temple one ข opens its loop inward at the top, the harbor one ค turns it outward. เขา (khǎo) — he or she — climbs because the temple one is doing the writing.",
+				"ถ sits flat like ท but coils its entry. ถาม (thǎam) is to ask; เรียน (riian) is to study — harbor ร opens it, so it stays level while ถาม rises.",
+				"ผ and ฝ are the bee and the lid: ฝ raises a taller stem than ผ, the way a lid stands above what it covers. ฝัน (fǎn) is to dream.",
+				"ส coils like ซ but lives uphill; สูง (sǔung) — tall — is its own reminder. เสีย (sǐa), to lose or to break, opens with it too."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "ia-vowel",
+			"heading": "เ-ีย — the ia glide",
+			"body": [
+				"เ-ีย wraps three signs around its consonant: เ in front, ี above, ย after. Read them as one long vowel, ia.",
+				"เสีย (sǐa) is that vowel under a temple s — live syllable, so it rises. เรียน (riian) is the same vowel under harbor ร — live again, but the harbor keeps it level.",

+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-cousin",
+			"prompt": "เขา (khǎo, he or she) rises. Respell it with harbor ค in place of ข and the climb disappears. Same kh sound, same vowel — what is the one written difference doing all of that work?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-cousin-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-cousin-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-cousin",
+			"answers": [
+				"The district. เขา is spelled with ข, the temple kh, and a temple letter on a live syllable gives rising tone. ค writes the identical sound from the harbor, where a live syllable stays mid."

+		},

+			"heading": "What you can now read",

@@ -0,0 +1,120 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-13",
+	"title": "The Sanskrit set",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "borrowed-letters",
+			"heading": "Six letters that mark a borrowed word",
+			"body": [
+				"Thai keeps extra letters for words it took from Sanskrit and Pali. They double sounds you already read, and seeing one is a hint that the word is old, formal, or borrowed.",
+				"ศ and ษ are temple s, like ส. ณ is harbor n, like น. ญ is harbor y, like ย. ภ is harbor ph, like พ. ธ is harbor th, like ท.",
+				"ศึกษา (sùek-sǎa) — to study — carries two of them at once. ภาพ (phâap) is a picture. เธอ (thooe) is you. คุณ (khun) — you, polite — ends on ณ."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "telling-them-apart",
+			"heading": "Reading the six on sight",
+			"body": [
+				"ศ leans forward with a split head; ษ carries a broken crown. Both live uphill in the temple.",
+				"ณ is น with a long tail folded under it. ญ is ย standing over a small base. ภ is a steep sail; ธ is a flag on a pole.",
+				"ญาติ (yâat) is a relative. เงิน (ngoen) is money — harbor ง, level tone, and a vowel written in a way this lesson explains below."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "high-dead-short-rule",
+			"ruleId": "high-dead-short"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "high-dead-long-rule",
+			"ruleId": "high-dead-long"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "temple-dead",
+			"heading": "The temple's other half: dead syllables fall low",
+			"body": [
+				"A temple letter on a live syllable rises — that was the last lesson. On a dead syllable it gives a low tone, short vowel or long.",
+				"หก (hòk) — six — is temple ห stopped by k: low. In ศึกษา (sùek-sǎa) the first half is temple ศ stopped by k, so it comes out low; the second half ends open and live, so it rises. One word, both temple rules."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "sara-am",
+			"heading": "ำ — the vowel with a built-in ending",
+			"body": [
+				"The sign ำ is a circle-then-hook written after its consonant, and it packs a vowel and a final m into one shape.",
+				"ทำ (tham) is to do. จำ (jam) is to remember. Both end in m with no ม written anywhere — the vowel brought its own."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "sara-am-rule",
+			"ruleId": "sara-am-properties"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "oe-vowel",
+			"heading": "เ-อ — the oe vowel, and the shape it takes before a final",
+			"body": [
+				"เ-อ wraps its consonant: เ in front, อ after. เธอ (thooe) is you; เจอ (jooe) is to meet.",
+				"Add a final consonant and the อ steps aside for ิ above: เงิน (ngoen), money, and เดิน (dooen), to walk, are เ-อ words in that closed shape.",
+				"The short mate เ-อะ clips it, and is rare in running text."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "gaaran-rule",
+			"ruleId": "gaaran"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "gaaran",
+			"heading": "The gaa-ran sign — the silencer",
+			"body": [
+				"Borrowed words often keep letters Thai does not say. The sign ์ above a letter switches it off.",
+				"สัตว์ (sàt) — animal — writes a ว and switches it off: a temple letter, a stopped ending, a low tone, and one letter kept purely for the eye."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "two-halves",
+			"prompt": "ศึกษา (to study) is read sùek-sǎa — low then rising. Both halves open with a temple s. What makes the two tones come out different?",
+			"revealSlideId": "two-halves-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "two-halves-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "two-halves",
+			"answers": [
+				"Live against dead. The first syllable is stopped by k — dead, so the temple gives it low. The second ends open on a long vowel — live, so the temple gives it rising."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "silent-letter",
+			"prompt": "สัตว์ (animal) is read sàt, one closed syllable. Its spelling ends with ว under a small sign. What is that sign doing, and what would the word lose without it?",
+			"revealSlideId": "silent-letter-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "silent-letter-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "silent-letter",
+			"answers": [
+				"That is gaa-ran, the silencer, switching off the ว. Without it the spelling would ask you to read the ว; with it the borrowed spelling survives on paper while the mouth says sàt."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "close",
+			"heading": "What you can now read",
+			"body": [
+				"The six loanword letters ศ ษ ณ ญ ภ ธ, the packed vowel ำ, เ-อ in both written shapes, and the silencer ์.",
+				"And the temple's tone behaviour is complete: rising when live, low when dead."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,98 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-14",
+	"title": "The rare tail",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-long-tail",
+			"heading": "Ten letters you will mostly wave at",
+			"body": [
+				"The alphabet has a long tail: ten letters that together carry less than one word in a hundred. You need to recognise them; you will rarely write them.",
+				"They are ฐ ฎ ฏ ฑ ฒ (mostly inside borrowed spellings), ฬ ฆ ฌ (rare doubles of ล ค ช), and ฃ ฅ — two letters modern Thai has retired outright.",
+				"The review queue schedules these at the lowest priority. They stay in the deck forever, but they will never crowd out the letters that carry the language."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "where-they-hide",
+			"heading": "Where the tail actually shows up",
+			"body": [
+				"ฐ, temple th, ends รัฐ (rát) — state — and opens ฐาน (thǎan) — base.",
+				"ฏ, market dt, sits inside ปฏิบัติ (bpà-dtì-bàt) — to carry out. ฎ is its market d twin, and both wear a crown-like base.",
+				"ฑ appears in บัณฑิต (ban-dìt) — a graduate. ฒ in พัฒนา (phát-thá-naa) — to develop. ฬ is the harbor l of กีฬา (gii-laa) — sport. ฆ opens โฆษณา (khôot-sà-naa) — advertising — and ends เมฆ (mêek) — cloud.",
+				"ฌ is the rarest consonant in the alphabet; outside a handful of ceremonial words you will meet it on charts and nowhere else."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "obsolete-rule",
+			"ruleId": "obsolete-consonants"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-retired-two",
+			"heading": "ฃ and ฅ — retired, still counted",
+			"body": [
+				"ฃ (temple kh) and ฅ (harbor kh) sit in every alphabet chart and in no modern word. Typewriters dropped them a century ago and the spellings that used them moved to ข and ค.",
+				"They are still letters of the alphabet, so they are still in your deck — at the very back of the queue."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "ua-uea",
+			"heading": "The last two vowel families",
+			"body": [
+				"-ัว is ua: ตัว (dtua) — body, or the classifier for animals — and หัว (hǔua) — head, rising on its temple ห.",
+				"เ-ือ is uea, three signs around one consonant: เสือ (sǔuea) is tiger, เรือ (ruuea) is boat, เดือน (duuean) is month, เมือง (muueang) is city or town.",
+				"Each has a clipped short mate, -ัวะ and เ-ือะ, both rare on the page."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "rare-vowel-signs",
+			"heading": "Four vowel signs that act like syllables",
+			"body": [
+				"ฤ writes r plus a short vowel in one sign: ฤดู (rúe-duu) is season, and อังกฤษ (ang-grìt) — English — hides it mid-word.",
+				"Lengthen it with ๅ and you get the long form; ฦ and its long form are its l-shaped mates, kept for completeness and effectively extinct.",
+				"Treat all four as spellings to recognise, not machinery to learn rules for."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "spot-the-rare",
+			"prompt": "เมฆ (cloud) is read mêek and falls. Its last letter is not the k you usually see. Which letter is it, and what does it tell you about the word?",
+			"revealSlideId": "spot-the-rare-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "spot-the-rare-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "spot-the-rare",
+			"answers": [
+				"ฆ, the rare harbor kh. As a final it just stops the syllable like any k — its real message is that เมฆ is a borrowed, bookish spelling, which is exactly where the tail letters live."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "crown-twins",
+			"prompt": "ฎ and ฏ are the crown-wearing twins of ด and ต. ปฏิบัติ uses one of them — which sound does the ฏ carry, and which district does it sit in?",
+			"revealSlideId": "crown-twins-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "crown-twins-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "crown-twins",
+			"answers": [
+				"ฏ is dt, exactly as ต is, and it sits in the market. The twins change no sound and no class — they only mark the word as an old borrowing."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "close",
+			"heading": "The alphabet is complete",
+			"body": [
+				"All forty-four consonants are now yours, every written vowel family, and the four rare signs. Nothing on a Thai page is an unknown shape any more.",
+				"What remains for the course is machinery, not letters: the vowels that are not written, the tone marks, clusters, and the leading consonants."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

@@ -0,0 +1,101 @@
+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-clusters",
+	"title": "Consonant clusters, true and false",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "only-three-followers",
+			"heading": "Only three letters ever come second",
+			"body": [
+				"English lets a syllable open with almost anything: str, spl, thw. Thai does not.",
+				"A Thai syllable can open with two consonants only when the second one is ร, ล or ว. No other letter has ever been second in a cluster.",
+				"And not every first letter is allowed either. The whole inventory is twenty pairs, and you are about to read all of them."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "true-clusters",
+			"heading": "Fifteen pairs where you say both letters",
+			"body": [
+				"With ร: กร, ขร, คร, ตร, ปร, พร. ตรง (dtrong) is straight, ครอง (khraawng) is to rule, ประตู (bprà-dtuu) is a door, พระ (phrá) is a monk, กรอบ (gràawp) is crisp.",
+				"With ล: กล, ขล, คล, ปล, ผล, พล. กลาง (glaang) is middle, กลับ (glàp) is to return, คลอง (khlaawng) is a canal, ปลา (bplaa) is a fish, ปลอม (bplaawm) is fake.",
+				"With ว: กว, ขว, คว. ความ (khwaam) makes a noun of whatever follows it, ขวา (khwǎa) is right, กว้าง (gwâang) is wide.",
+				"Speak both, left to right, with no vowel wedged between them. A pair always takes its class from the first letter."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "false-sound-clusters",
+			"heading": "Two pairs that are not what they look like",
+			"body": [
+				"ทร is read as s. ทราบ (sâap) is to know, ทรง (song) is a form, ทราย (saai) is sand. It is never thr.",
+				"ซร is read as s too, and you will meet it about once.",
+				"The sound changes but the class does not: ท is low class and ทราบ takes its tone from ท."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "silent-second-clusters",
+			"heading": "Three pairs where the ร is silent",
+			"body": [
+				"จร, ศร and สร drop the ร entirely. Say the first letter and go straight on to the vowel.",
+				"จริง (jing) is true, and สร้าง (sâang) is to build. Neither has an r in it anywhere."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "lexical-pairs",
+			"heading": "ผล and พล are decided by the word, not by the spelling",
+			"body": [
+				"ผลิต (phà-lìt) is to manufacture and ผลไม้ (phǒn-lá-máai) is fruit. Neither is a cluster: ผ is a separate light syllable in the first and ผล is a bare pair in the second.",
+				"พลัง (phá-lang) is power and is not a cluster either, while พลอย (phlaawi) is a gemstone and is.",
+				"These two pairs are the only place in the inventory where the page will not tell you. Learn the word."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "is-it-a-cluster",
+			"prompt": "ถนน opens with ถ followed by น. Is that a cluster, and how do you know without knowing the word?",
+			"revealSlideId": "is-it-a-cluster-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "is-it-a-cluster-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "is-it-a-cluster",
+			"answers": [
+				"No. น is not ร, ล or ว, so ถน cannot be a cluster and no list needs consulting.",
+				"The two letters belong to different syllables, and ถ takes a short a of its own."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "consonant-clusters",
+			"ruleId": "consonant-clusters"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-closure",
+			"heading": "Twenty pairs, and nothing else",
+			"body": [
+				"Fifteen true, two read as s, three that drop the ร. That is the entire inventory, and it does not grow.",
+				"Any other two consonants standing together are two syllables, not one opening. There is no judgement call and no borderline case to weigh.",
+				"This is why the inventory is worth the twenty lines it takes: it is the only way to know that ขน in ขนาด is not a cluster, and that ขว in ขวา is."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-tone-decides",
+			"prompt": "ทราบ opens with a pair read as s, and ท is low class while ส is high class. Which of the two decides the tone?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-tone-decides-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-tone-decides-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-tone-decides",
+			"answers": [
+				"ท does. The sound changed; the class did not.",
+				"ท is low class and the syllable is long and dead, which is falling tone: sâap."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-leading-consonants",
+	"title": "Leading consonants: อักษรนำ",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "why-it-exists",
+			"heading": "Ten letters that cannot be written with a rising tone",
+			"body": [
+				"ง ญ ณ น ม ย ร ล ว ฬ are the sonorants: the ten letters you can hold and hum.",
+				"Every one of them is low class, and none has a high or mid class twin the way ค has ข.",
+				"A low class letter on its own can reach mid, falling and high tone, and that is all. Rising tone and low tone are simply not spellable on it.",
+				"Thai solves this by putting another letter in front. That front letter is not there to be heard. It is there to be a class."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "one-rule",
+			"heading": "The rule, once",
+			"body": [
+				"A mid or high class consonant written directly in front of a sonorant leads it, and hands its class to the syllable the sonorant opens.",
+				"Nothing else changes. The vowel, the final and the live or dead reading are whatever the written syllable says they are; only the class comes from outside.",
+				"Everything below is this one sentence meeting three different first letters. It is not three rules."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "branch-silent-h",
+			"heading": "First letter ห, and you do not hear it",
+			"body": [
+				"หมด (mòt) is finished, หลง (lǒng) is to be lost, หนัง (nǎng) is a film, หญิง (yǐng) is a woman, หมอ (mǎaw) is a doctor, หรอก (ràawk) softens a denial.",
+				"There is no h in any of them. ห in this position is written and never spoken.",
+				"Any of the ten may follow it, and new words still take it, so treat this as open."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "branch-silent-o",
+			"heading": "First letter อ, four words, no more",
+			"body": [
+				"อย่า (yàa) is don't. อยู่ (yùu) is to stay. อย่าง (yàang) is a kind or sort. อยาก (yàak) is to want. That is the complete list.",
+				"อ in front of ย is silent here, exactly as ห is.",
+				"There is no fifth word and no fifth is coming. Read ยาก and ยาว as the low class ย they are, because nothing precedes them."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "branch-spoken-leader",
+			"heading": "Any other mid or high first letter, and you do hear it",
+			"body": [
+				"สวัสดี (sà-wàt-dii) at rank nine is this branch, and so are ขนาด (khà-nàat), ตลอด (dtà-làawt), สงบ (sà-ngòp), สมัย (sà-mǎi), ผลิต (phà-lìt) and ถนน (thà-nǒn).",
+				"Here the first letter keeps its own sound. It takes the short a of a consonant that will not fit, and becomes a light syllable ahead of the main one.",
+				"ตลก (dtà-lòk), ขนม (khà-nǒm), สบาย (sà-baai), ตลาด (dtà-làat) and ฉลาด (chà-làat) are the same shape. This branch is wide open and you will meet it daily."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "two-first-letters",
+			"prompt": "หมด begins with ห and ตลก begins with ต. In one of them the first letter is spoken and in the other it is not. What is the same about the two words?",
+			"revealSlideId": "two-first-letters-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "two-first-letters-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "two-first-letters",
+			"answers": [
+				"In both, the letter in front is the one the tone is worked out from, and the letter after it is not.",
+				"Spoken or not spoken: that is all that separates one branch from the next."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "hor-nam",
+			"ruleId": "hor-nam"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "not-every-pair",
+			"heading": "When the first letter is simply the initial",
+			"body": [
+				"สนใจ (sǒn-jai) has ส in front of น and is one syllable, not two: สน is a bare pair with a short o, and ส is its own initial.",
+				"Count syllables the shorter way first. Only when a letter cannot be read into the syllable beside it does it become a leader.",
+				"And a low class first letter never leads at all. It has no class the sonorant does not already have, so นคร is ná-khaawn with two ordinary syllables."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-tone",
+			"prompt": "หมด and มด are both real words, both read with a short o and a d that stops the air. Why do they not have the same tone?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-tone-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-tone-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-tone",
+			"answers": [
+				"มด (mót) is high tone, because ม is low class and the syllable is short and dead.",
+				"หมด (mòt) is low tone, because the ห in front makes the reading a high class one."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-numerals",
+	"title": "Thai numerals, ๐ through ๙",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "why-optional",
+			"heading": "Ten glyphs, entirely optional",
+			"body": [
+				"Thailand writes numbers with Arabic digits almost everywhere. The Thai digits survive on official documents, temple signs, some price boards — and anywhere a date wants to look formal.",
+				"Skipping this lesson skips nothing else: no later material depends on it, and the course is complete without it. It waits here if a menu ever charges you the Thai-digit price."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "zero-to-four",
+			"heading": "Zero through four: ๐ ๑ ๒ ๓ ๔",
+			"body": [
+				"๐ is zero, a plain ring — ศูนย์ (sǔun), a word you already can read: temple ศ up front and a silenced ย at the end.",
+				"๑ is one, หนึ่ง (nùeng). ๒ is two, สอง (sǎawng). ๓ is three, สาม (sǎam) — the two and three share a base; three carries an extra hump.",
+				"๔ is four, สี่ (sìi), and its glyph forks like a flag."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "five-to-nine",
+			"heading": "Five through nine, ๕ to ๙",
+			"body": [
+				"๕ is five, ห้า (hâa) — the glyph coils back on itself. ๖ is six, หก (hòk).",
+				"๗ is seven, เจ็ด (jèt), and ๘ is eight, แปด (bpàaet) — a matched pair of hooks facing opposite ways.",
+				"๙ is nine, เก้า (gâo), with a tail that climbs. Larger units are ordinary words: สิบ (sìp) ten, ร้อย (ráawi) hundred, พัน (phan) thousand, ล้าน (láan) million."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "reading-a-number",
+			"heading": "Reading a number you meet on a sign",
+			"body": [
+				"Thai digits combine exactly as Arabic ones do — position by position, nothing reordered.",
+				"๒๕ is 25. ๑๐๐ is 100. A ticket stamped ๗๕ is asking for 75, and the only new skill is glyph recognition.",
+				"The word เลข (lêek) — number — is what signs use to label them."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "read-price",
+			"prompt": "A market stall lists a price as ๓๕. What number is that, and which two digit glyphs did you just read?",
+			"revealSlideId": "read-price-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "read-price-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "read-price",
+			"answers": [
+				"35. ๓ is three — the humped glyph — and ๕ is five, the one that coils back on itself. Position works exactly as in Arabic digits."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "spot-digit",
+			"prompt": "๙ and ๗ both rise to a point. A date stamp reads ๙. Which number is it, and what tells the two glyphs apart?",
+			"revealSlideId": "spot-digit-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "spot-digit-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "spot-digit",
+			"answers": [
+				"Nine. ๙ finishes with a tail that climbs above the line, while ๗ keeps a straight neck with a small hook."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "close",
+			"heading": "Done — or happily skipped",
+			"body": [
+				"Ten glyphs, their number words, and positional reading. Whether you learned them or skipped them, the course stands complete behind you."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+{
+	"lessonId": "lesson-tone-marks",
+	"title": "The eight-cell tone-mark table, at once",
+	"slides": [
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "one-table",
+			"heading": "One table, twelve cells, three districts",
+			"body": [
+				"Every consonant already carries a class — market, harbor or temple — and that class alone decides a syllable's tone with no mark written at all.",
+				"A tone mark changes that outcome, and there are only four shapes: mai ek (่), mai tho (้), mai tri (๊) and mai chattawa (๋).",
+				"Lay all three classes against all four marks and you get twelve cells. Eight occur in standard spelling. The other four do not, and that absence is a fact worth learning, not a gap to skip past."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "mid-class-marks",
+			"heading": "The market takes all four, in order",
+			"body": [
+				"mai ek (่) gives low tone. ไก่ (gài) is chicken.",
+				"mai tho (้) gives falling tone. เก้า (gâo) is nine.",
+				"mai tri (๊) gives high tone, and the market is the only district that ever takes this mark. โต๊ะ (dtó) is a table.",
+				"mai chattawa (๋) gives rising tone, market only again. เดี๋ยว (dǐao) is \"in a moment.\"",
+				"Four marks, and each lands on a different tone of its own — the market is the whole set, spoken for."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "high-class-marks",
+			"heading": "The temple takes two",
+			"body": [
+				"mai ek (่) gives low tone here too. ข่าว (khàao) is news.",
+				"mai tho (้) gives falling tone. ให้ (hâi) is to give.",
+				"mai tri and mai chattawa never sit over a temple letter in standard spelling. The shapes are writable — they turn up in loanwords and informal spelling — but no standard word pairs either one with a temple letter."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "low-class-marks",
+			"heading": "The harbor takes two, and swaps them",
+			"body": [
+				"mai ek (่) gives falling tone here — the opposite of what it gave the temple. ล่าง (lâang) is below.",
+				"mai tho (้) gives high tone here — again the opposite of the temple's falling. ม้า (máa) is horse.",
+				"The harbor is the odd one out in the whole table: the same two marks that gave the temple low-then-falling give the harbor falling-then-high.",
+				"Mai tri and mai chattawa never sit over a harbor letter either, for the same reason as the temple: not used in standard spelling."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-tone-a",
+			"prompt": "ตั๋ว (dtǔua, ticket) carries mai chattawa over ต. What tone does it give, and why does the answer not need the temple or harbor rows at all?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-tone-a-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-tone-a-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-tone-a",
+			"answers": [
+				"Rising. ต is market class, and the market is the only district mai chattawa ever appears in — so there is only one row to check, and the other two districts never come up."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "retrieval",
+			"id": "which-tone-b",
+			"prompt": "ล่าง (lâang, below) carries mai ek over ล, a harbor letter. The market's mai ek gives low tone. Does ล่าง come out low too?",
+			"revealSlideId": "which-tone-b-answer"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "reveal",
+			"id": "which-tone-b-answer",
+			"retrievalSlideId": "which-tone-b",
+			"answers": [
+				"No. The harbor is the exception: its mai ek gives falling, not low. ล่าง is falling tone — the opposite of what the same mark gives the temple."
+			]
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "tone-mark-placement",
+			"ruleId": "tone-mark-placement"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "rule",
+			"id": "mai-tri-chattawa-scope",
+			"ruleId": "mai-tri-chattawa-middle-only"
+		},
+		{
+			"kind": "exposition",
+			"id": "the-shape-of-the-table",
+			"heading": "What makes eight cells memorable",
+			"body": [
+				"The market takes all four marks, each one a different tone: mai ek for low, mai tho for falling, mai tri for high, mai chattawa for rising.",
+				"The temple and the harbor only ever take mai ek and mai tho — the other two marks belong to the market alone.",
+				"And the harbor is the one that flips: the same two marks that give the temple low-then-falling give the harbor falling-then-high."
+			]
+		}
+	]
+}

+import { readdirSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";

+} from "./symbolPriority";
+import { consonants } from "./symbols";
+
+const SRC_ROOT = join(import.meta.dirname, "..", "..", "..");
+
+function sourceFiles(dir: string): string[] {
+	return readdirSync(dir, { withFileTypes: true }).flatMap((entry) => {
+		const path = join(dir, entry.name);
+		if (entry.isDirectory()) return sourceFiles(path);
+		if (!/\.tsx?$/.test(entry.name)) return [];
+		if (/\.test\.tsx?$/.test(entry.name)) return [];
+		return [path];
+	});
+}
+
+function countMatches(pattern: RegExp): number {
+	return sourceFiles(SRC_ROOT).reduce((total, path) => {
+		const matches = readFileSync(path, "utf8").match(pattern);
+		return total + (matches ? matches.length : 0);
+	}, 0);
+}
+
+describe("AC4 — one priority declaration site repo-wide", () => {

+		expect(countMatches(/readonly priority\?: number/g)).toBe(1);
+	});

+	it("declares no second priority array in symbolPriority.ts itself", () => {
+		const source = readFileSync(

+		expect(source).not.toMatch(/priority:\s*\d+/);
+	});
+
+	it("reads ThaiConsonant.priority directly rather than a parallel map", () => {
+		for (const consonant of consonants) {
+			expect(getSchedulingPriority(consonant.character)).toBe(

+			);
+		}
+	});

+		];
+		const frequency = computeAnyPositionFrequency(entries);
+		expect(frequency.get("ก")).toBe(2);
+	});

+	it("matches the declared symbols.ts priority for every consonant", () => {

+		for (const consonant of consonants) {

+	it("gives the most frequent consonant the highest priority (rank 1)", () => {

+		const derived = deriveConsonantPriority(frequency);

--- /dev/null
+++ w/src/domain/script/data/symbolPriority.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,81 @@
+/**
+ * Scheduling priority for the 44 consonants (Task 4.1).
+ *
+ * CONTEXT.md rule 2 — build on, never beside. `ThaiConsonant.priority` (and
+ * the field on the other symbol subclasses) already exists at 98 sites; this
+ * module is the field's first consumer, not a second priority concept. There
+ * is exactly one place the optional numeric priority field is declared, in
+ * `symbols.ts` — asserted by `lessonSequence.test.ts`'s
+ * "declares symbol priority exactly once" case and re-asserted here against
+ * the derivation this module owns.
+ *
+ * Demotion changes what a letter's `priority` number IS, computed from
+ * corpus frequency, never whether the letter is in the set: the count of
+ * consonants is unaffected (AC6).
+ */
+
+import vocabularyData from "../../vocabulary/data/vocabulary.json";
+import { consonants } from "./symbols";
+
+interface CorpusEntry {
+	readonly characters?: readonly string[];
+}
+
+const CONSONANT_CHARACTERS: readonly string[] = consonants.map(
+	(consonant) => consonant.character,
+);
+
+/**
+ * Any-position occurrence count across the vocabulary corpus: every
+ * character slot in every entry's `characters` array, not just word-initial
+ * position (AC5). An initial-position count would demote letters that are
+ * common medially or finally but rare as an initial — measured, seven of the
+ * ten letters this phase demotes still appear in the corpus's top-600 words.
+ */
+export function computeAnyPositionFrequency(
+	entries: readonly CorpusEntry[] = vocabularyData as CorpusEntry[],
+): Map<string, number> {
+	const counts = new Map<string, number>(
+		CONSONANT_CHARACTERS.map((character) => [character, 0]),
+	);
+	for (const entry of entries) {
+		for (const character of entry.characters ?? []) {
+			if (counts.has(character)) {
+				counts.set(character, (counts.get(character) ?? 0) + 1);
+			}
+		}
+	}
+	return counts;
+}
+
+/**
+ * Rank order derived from corpus frequency: rank 1 is the most frequent
+ * consonant, rank 44 the rarest. Ties break on the character itself (plain
+ * code-point order) so the derivation is deterministic and reproducible from
+ * the corpus alone — never hand-curated.
+ */
+export function deriveConsonantPriority(
+	frequency: Map<string, number> = computeAnyPositionFrequency(),
+): Map<string, number> {
+	const ranked = [...CONSONANT_CHARACTERS].sort((a, b) => {
+		const byFrequency = (frequency.get(b) ?? 0) - (frequency.get(a) ?? 0);
+		if (byFrequency !== 0) return byFrequency;
+		return a < b ? -1 : a > b ? 1 : 0;
+	});
+	return new Map(ranked.map((character, index) => [character, index + 1]));
+}
+
+/**
+ * The scheduling priority for a consonant — reads `ThaiConsonant.priority`
+ * directly, the single declaration site. Rare letters get a larger number
+ * (lower priority) without leaving the symbol set.
+ */
+export function getSchedulingPriority(character: string): number | undefined {
+	return consonants.find((consonant) => consonant.character === character)
+		?.priority;
+}
+
+/** The number of consonants in the SRS. Demotion must never change this. */
+export function consonantCount(): number {
+	return consonants.length;
+}

diff --git c/src/domain/script/data/toneMarkTable.ts w/src/domain/script/data/toneMarkTable.ts
new file mode 100644
index 00000000..334a0e4a
--- /dev/null
+++ w/src/domain/script/data/toneMarkTable.ts
@@ -0,0 +1,155 @@
+/**
+ * The eight-cell tone-mark table as one checkable structure (Task 4.1).
+ *
+ * The source course spreads mid class (lessons 17-18), high class (21-22) and
+ * low class (23-24) across six lessons with unrelated material between them.
+ * The table is small enough to teach as one pattern: mid class takes all four
+ * marks; high and low class take only mái-èek and mái-thoo; low class is the
+ * odd one out, giving falling/high where high class gives low/falling.
+ *
+ * CONTEXT.md rule 2 — build on, never beside. `completeToneChart.withToneMark`
+ * already carries this exact table, with `"N/A"` recording the four
+ * combinations standard spelling never uses. This module reads that chart and
+ * `toneMarkRules` rather than re-declaring the data, and turns the "N/A"
+ * shorthand into a queryable three-state result (AC7): a class-and-mark
+ * combination is `"resolved"`, declared `"unreachable"`, or `"undeclared"` —
+ * three distinct states, so an unimplemented query never reads the same as an
+ * impossible one.
+ *
+ * `"unreachable"`, not `"impossible"` (AC2): mái-dtrii and mái-jàt-dtà-waa on
+ * a high- or low-class consonant are writable shapes that turn up in
+ * loanwords and informal spelling. They are absent from *standard*
+ * orthography, which is a fact about spelling convention, not about what a
+ * learner could be shown and told "that can't exist."
+ */
+
+import {
+	completeToneChart,
+	ThaiSymbolClass,
+	type ToneMarkRule,
+	type ToneValue,
+	toneMarkRules,
+	toneRules,
+} from "./symbols";
+
+export type ToneMarkName = "mai ek" | "mai tho" | "mai tri" | "mai chattawa";
+
+export const TONE_MARK_NAMES: readonly ToneMarkName[] = Object.freeze([
+	"mai ek",
+	"mai tho",
+	"mai tri",
+	"mai chattawa",
+]);
+
+export const TONE_MARK_TABLE_CLASSES: readonly ThaiSymbolClass[] =
+	Object.freeze([
+		ThaiSymbolClass.Mid,
+		ThaiSymbolClass.High,
+		ThaiSymbolClass.Low,
+	]);
+
+export type ToneMarkCellState = "resolved" | "unreachable" | "undeclared";
+
+export interface ToneMarkCell {
+	readonly toneMarkName: ToneMarkName;
+	readonly consonantClass: ThaiSymbolClass;
+	readonly state: ToneMarkCellState;
+	readonly resultingTone?: ToneValue;
+	/** Present only when `state` is `"unreachable"`. */
+	readonly note?: string;
+}
+
+const UNREACHABLE_NOTE =
+	"Not used in standard spelling. The shape is writable — it appears in loanwords and informal spelling — but no standard word pairs this mark with this consonant class.";
+
+function findRule(
+	toneMarkName: ToneMarkName,
+	consonantClass: ThaiSymbolClass,
+): ToneMarkRule | undefined {
+	return toneMarkRules.find(
+		(rule) =>
+			rule.toneMarkName === toneMarkName &&
+			rule.consonantClass === consonantClass,
+	);
+}
+
+/**
+ * `completeToneChart.withToneMark.rules` records `"N/A"` for mid-only marks
+ * against the `high`/`low` columns — that IS the unreachable set, read off
+ * the existing chart rather than re-declared.
+ */
+function isDeclaredUnreachable(
+	toneMarkName: ToneMarkName,
+	consonantClass: ThaiSymbolClass,
+): boolean {
+	if (consonantClass === ThaiSymbolClass.Mid) return false;
+	const column = consonantClass === ThaiSymbolClass.High ? "high" : "low";
+	const row = completeToneChart.withToneMark.rules.find((candidate) =>
+		candidate.mark.startsWith(toneMarkName),
+	);
+	return row?.[column] === "N/A";
+}
+
+/** AC1, AC2, AC7 — every class-and-mark combination resolves to exactly one
+ * of three states, and "unreachable" is a declaration, not an absence. */
+export function getToneMarkCell(
+	toneMarkName: ToneMarkName,
+	consonantClass: ThaiSymbolClass,
+): ToneMarkCell {
+	const rule = findRule(toneMarkName, consonantClass);
+	if (rule) {
+		return {
+			toneMarkName,
+			consonantClass,
+			state: "resolved",
+			resultingTone: rule.resultingTone,
+		};
+	}
+	if (isDeclaredUnreachable(toneMarkName, consonantClass)) {
+		return {
+			toneMarkName,
+			consonantClass,
+			state: "unreachable",
+			note: UNREACHABLE_NOTE,
+		};
+	}
+	return { toneMarkName, consonantClass, state: "undeclared" };
+}
+
+/** The full 3-class × 4-mark table the lesson renders — twelve cells. */
+export function buildToneMarkTable(): ToneMarkCell[] {
+	return TONE_MARK_TABLE_CLASSES.flatMap((consonantClass) =>
+		TONE_MARK_NAMES.map((toneMarkName) =>
+			getToneMarkCell(toneMarkName, consonantClass),
+		),
+	);
+}
+
+export interface SyllableToneQuery {
+	/** The syllable's governing class — for a leading-consonant syllable this
+	 * is the leader's class, not the class of the letter the mark sits over
+	 * (AC3). */
+	readonly governingClass: ThaiSymbolClass;
+	readonly syllableType: "live" | "dead-short" | "dead-long";
+	readonly toneMark?: ToneMarkName;
+}
+
+/**
+ * AC3 — a tone mark resolves against the governing class and, once resolved,
+ * the live/dead spelling rule (`toneRules`) is not consulted at all: the mark
+ * wins outright rather than being weighed against the spelling outcome.
+ */
+export function resolveSyllableTone(
+	query: SyllableToneQuery,
+): ToneValue | undefined {
+	if (query.toneMark) {
+		const cell = getToneMarkCell(query.toneMark, query.governingClass);
+		if (cell.state === "resolved") return cell.resultingTone;
+	}
+	const spellingRule = toneRules.find(
+		(rule) =>
+			rule.consonantClass === query.governingClass &&
+			rule.syllableType === query.syllableType,
+	);
+	return spellingRule?.resultingTone;
+}

+// @vitest-environment jsdom
+import { screen } from "@testing-library/react";

+import { renderWithApp, stubDeckJson } from "../test-utils/renderWithApp";
+import { LessonPage } from "./LessonPage";
+
+function renderAt(position: number) {
+	return renderWithApp(
+		<Routes>
+			<Route path="/lesson/:lessonNumber" element={<LessonPage />} />
+		</Routes>,
+		{},
+		{ route: `/lesson/${position}` },
+	);
+}
+
+describe("LessonPage — content resolution keys off position, not legacy number", () => {
+	// Task 4.3's resequence made `position` and `legacyNumber` diverge from
+	// position 15 on (`lessonSequence.ts`'s `lessonEntryByPosition` doc
+	// comment). `LessonPage` used to look content up with
+	// `lessonEntryByNumber(num)` — the legacy-number lookup — against `num`,
+	// which is actually the URL's *position*. For any position past 14 that
+	// silently misresolves to "undeclared", even though
+	// `lesson.getScriptSummary` (routed through `entryAt`, position-based
+	// throughout) already found the lesson fine. Task 6.2 fixed the call to
+	// `lessonEntryByPosition`; this pins it so a regression shows up as a
+	// broken lesson page rather than as a silent divergence again.
+	it("renders the deck for position 15 (lesson-unwritten-vowels, legacy number 26)", async () => {
+		stubDeckJson("/thai-script/lessons/lesson-unwritten-vowels/deck.json", {
+			lessonId: "lesson-unwritten-vowels",
+			title: "Vowels That Are Not Written",
+			slides: [
+				{
+					kind: "exposition",
+					id: "s1",
+					heading: "Unwritten vowels",
+					body: ["A vowel a lesson doesn't spell."],
+				},
+				{
+					kind: "retrieval",
+					id: "try",
+					prompt:
+						"How many consonants with nothing between them imply a short o?",
+					revealSlideId: "show",
+				},
+				{
+					kind: "reveal",
+					id: "show",
+					retrievalSlideId: "try",
+					answers: ["two"],
+				},
+			],
+		});
+
+		renderAt(15);
+
+		// Never the undeclared/unresolvable error branch: that branch shows
+		// this exact copy instead of a heading matching the summary.
+		expect(screen.queryByText("Lesson not found")).toBeNull();
+		expect(await screen.findByText("Unwritten vowels")).toBeTruthy();
+		expect(screen.getByText("Lesson 15")).toBeTruthy();
+	});
+});

89	# Task 1.1b — The five-store migration
90	
91	The hazardous half. CONTEXT.md's Rule 1 is the whole brief: five persisted
92	stores key on lesson number, `tsc` catches none of it because every side is
93	`number`, and 295 of 295 cards in the repo's own `progress.json` carry store 5.
94	
95	Migrate all five **in one pass**, at the boundary the repo already has.
96	
97	## Acceptance Criteria
98	
99	- AC1: All five stores convert together: `completedLessons`, `currentLesson`,
100	  `sym.lesson`, the lessons table's `number`, and `ScriptPropertyCard.lessonNumber`
101	  on every persisted card. A fixture carrying all five converts in one load, and
102	  a fixture carrying only some is reported rather than half-converted.
103	- AC2: The conversion runs inside `Storage.ts`'s existing `migrateState`, the
104	  repo's established migrate-once-at-load boundary. No second migration site is
105	  introduced, and no consumer carries its own back-compatibility branch.
106	- AC3: For the same learner, `getUnlockedWords()` returns the same words before
107	  and after migration. This is the join-key proof, asserted through the
108	  **public** method — `getMasteredCharacters` is `private` on a class exported
109	  as `VocabularyService`, and `getMasteredToneRules` gates the same result, so
110	  asserting the public output covers both.
111	- AC4: `MergeService` unions two devices' state when one input is migrated and
112	  the other is not, losing nothing from either side, across all five stores.
113	- AC5: Three persisted states are distinguishable: never written, written and
114	  empty, and written but unreadable (reported with its reason). Unreadable never
115	  reads as empty.
116	- AC6: No lesson-count literal remains in `ScriptLessonService.ts`,
117	  `AchievementService.ts`, `ProgressPage.tsx` (both sites) or
118	  `AchievementBadge.tsx`. Each derives from the declared sequence, including the
119	  badge's user-facing copy.
120	- AC7: All three integer walks read the declared sequence rather than
121	  `1..n`: `startLesson`, `getNextLesson`, and `LessonPath`'s node enumeration.
122	  `LessonPath` renders one node per declared lesson, whatever the count.
123	- AC8: The Playwright suite passes. Its assertions are updated where this plan
124	  legitimately changes behaviour, and the suite is in this task's `verify` so
125	  the change is visible to a gate.
126	- AC9: `startLesson` enforces prerequisites from the declared order. A lesson
127	  with an incomplete predecessor is refused, naming that predecessor.
128	
129	## Test cases
130	
131	- A five-store fixture converts in one load; re-saving and re-loading is stable.
132	- A fixture with `completedLessons` migrated but `lessonNumber` not is reported,
133	  not silently accepted — the half-migrated state is the hazard.
134	- `getUnlockedWords()` is identical across migration for a learner part-way
135	  through, not only for empty and complete learners.
136	- Two states, one migrated and one not, merge to the union across all five.
137	- Never-written, empty and unreadable are three distinct reports.
138	- Grepping the five named files finds no lesson-count integer literal.
139	- `LessonPath` with a 20-lesson sequence renders 20 nodes; with 25, 25.
140	- The achievement badge's label and its unlock condition agree, at any count.
141	- `startLesson` names the first incomplete predecessor.
142	
143	## Architectural Decision
144	
145	**One pass at `migrateState`, never per consumer.** The repo already implements
146	this pattern at `Storage.ts:40`; a second boundary would leave two migration
147	sites disagreeing about which shape is current. CONTEXT.md records per-consumer
148	back-compatibility as the bug shape rather than the fix.
149	
150	**The count literals are converted here, not "later."** Five literals across
151	four files and three layers decide achievement eligibility, the progress
152	display, the badge's copy, and which lesson the app offers next. They exist
153	because the count has nowhere else to live; 1.1a gives it a home, so this task
154	moves them all at once. Updating them to `20` instead would relocate the
155	problem to phase 4's resequencing.
156	
157	**`e2e/` enters a `covers` for the first time.** The Playwright suite asserts
158	Lesson 1 shows a `<video>` and checks a romanization this plan changes. It is
159	excluded from vitest and no `verify` ran it, so the plan would have broken it
160	invisibly. Owning it here makes the breakage a gate failure rather than a
161	discovery.
162	
163	*Rejected:* migrating stores 1–4 and leaving `lessonNumber` to a later task.
164	That is precisely the half-migration this plan opens by warning about, and it
165	would silently change every learner's mastered-character set.
166

# Task 1.1b — The five-store migration

The hazardous half. CONTEXT.md's Rule 1 is the whole brief: five persisted
stores key on lesson number, `tsc` catches none of it because every side is
`number`, and 295 of 295 cards in the repo's own `progress.json` carry store 5.

Migrate all five **in one pass**, at the boundary the repo already has.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1: All five stores convert together: `completedLessons`, `currentLesson`,
  `sym.lesson`, the lessons table's `number`, and `ScriptPropertyCard.lessonNumber`
  on every persisted card. A fixture carrying all five converts in one load, and
  a fixture carrying only some is reported rather than half-converted.
- AC2: The conversion runs inside `Storage.ts`'s existing `migrateState`, the
  repo's established migrate-once-at-load boundary. No second migration site is
  introduced, and no consumer carries its own back-compatibility branch.
- AC3: For the same learner, `getUnlockedWords()` returns the same words before
  and after migration. This is the join-key proof, asserted through the
  **public** method — `getMasteredCharacters` is `private` on a class exported
  as `VocabularyService`, and `getMasteredToneRules` gates the same result, so
  asserting the public output covers both.
- AC4: `MergeService` unions two devices' state when one input is migrated and
  the other is not, losing nothing from either side, across all five stores.
- AC5: Three persisted states are distinguishable: never written, written and
  empty, and written but unreadable (reported with its reason). Unreadable never
  reads as empty.
- AC6: No lesson-count literal remains in `ScriptLessonService.ts`,
  `AchievementService.ts`, `ProgressPage.tsx` (both sites) or
  `AchievementBadge.tsx`. Each derives from the declared sequence, including the
  badge's user-facing copy.
- AC7: All three integer walks read the declared sequence rather than
  `1..n`: `startLesson`, `getNextLesson`, and `LessonPath`'s node enumeration.
  `LessonPath` renders one node per declared lesson, whatever the count.
- AC8: The Playwright suite passes. Its assertions are updated where this plan
  legitimately changes behaviour, and the suite is in this task's `verify` so
  the change is visible to a gate.
- AC9: `startLesson` enforces prerequisites from the declared order. A lesson
  with an incomplete predecessor is refused, naming that predecessor.

## Test cases

- A five-store fixture converts in one load; re-saving and re-loading is stable.
- A fixture with `completedLessons` migrated but `lessonNumber` not is reported,
  not silently accepted — the half-migrated state is the hazard.
- `getUnlockedWords()` is identical across migration for a learner part-way
  through, not only for empty and complete learners.
- Two states, one migrated and one not, merge to the union across all five.
- Never-written, empty and unreadable are three distinct reports.
- Grepping the five named files finds no lesson-count integer literal.
- `LessonPath` with a 20-lesson sequence renders 20 nodes; with 25, 25.
- The achievement badge's label and its unlock condition agree, at any count.
- `startLesson` names the first incomplete predecessor.

## Architectural Decision

**One pass at `migrateState`, never per consumer.** The repo already implements
this pattern at `Storage.ts:40`; a second boundary would leave two migration
sites disagreeing about which shape is current. CONTEXT.md records per-consumer
back-compatibility as the bug shape rather than the fix.

**The count literals are converted here, not "later."** Five literals across
four files and three layers decide achievement eligibility, the progress
display, the badge's copy, and which lesson the app offers next. They exist
because the count has nowhere else to live; 1.1a gives it a home, so this task
moves them all at once. Updating them to `20` instead would relocate the
problem to phase 4's resequencing.

**`e2e/` enters a `covers` for the first time.** The Playwright suite asserts
Lesson 1 shows a `<video>` and checks a romanization this plan changes. It is
excluded from vitest and no `verify` ran it, so the plan would have broken it
invisibly. Owning it here makes the breakage a gate failure rather than a
discovery.

*Rejected:* migrating stores 1–4 and leaving `lessonNumber` to a later task.
That is precisely the half-migration this plan opens by warning about, and it
would silently change every learner's mastered-character set.

# Task 1.3 — The deck generation pipeline

A lesson script in, a deck plus its committed assets out. Read
`scripts/generate-sentence-audio.py`'s docstring first: it records the
verification discipline this pipeline reuses and several levers that are not
levers.

Narration is English prose with Thai embedded. The script marks spans `en` or
`th`; **both go to ElevenLabs**, but Thai spans additionally pass a
transcribe-back check before their clip is accepted, because a wrong tone
teaches a mispronunciation and the tone lessons are the product.

## Acceptance Criteria

- AC1: Given a lesson script, the generator emits deck JSON that validates
  against the schema from task 1.1, with one slide per declared slide and an
  asset reference per generated clip and image.
- AC2: Audio and images are cached by a hash of their inputs (segment text,
  voice id, model, settings). Re-running against an unchanged script issues no
  API calls; changing one segment regenerates that segment's clip and leaves the
  rest byte-identical. The manifest records each asset's hash.
- AC3: With no API key in the environment, the generator exits non-zero
  naming the missing variable. It never emits a deck with silently absent audio,
  and never falls back to a partial run that reads as a success.
- AC4: Every asset path written or referenced resolves inside
  `public/lessons/<lessonId>/`. A lesson id outside the charset task 1.1
  declares, or a path escaping that directory, is refused before any write.
- AC5: The API key never reaches deck JSON, the manifest, a committed file,
  or the generator's own stdout — including inside an error message echoed from
  the API.
- AC6: A Thai segment's clip is transcribed back before acceptance; a
  mismatch is retried, and a clip still failing after retries is recorded as
  failed rather than shipped. The manifest carries each Thai clip's verification
  outcome.
- AC7: Every segment in the manifest is in exactly one of three states —
  never generated, generated, or generation failed — and the three are distinct
  values. A failed segment is never recorded as absent.

## Test cases

- A committed fixture deck validates against the schema.
- Every asset path in the fixture resolves under its own lesson directory; a
  crafted deck with `../` in an asset path is refused.
- A lesson id with an uppercase letter, a slash, or 65 characters is refused.
- The manifest's recorded hash for each asset matches the committed file.
- Scanning committed deck JSON and manifest finds nothing matching an API-key
  shape.
- The manifest's three segment states are three distinct values, and a failed
  segment is not serialised as a missing one.

## Architectural Decision

**Evidence lands in vitest, not a new Python test runner.** The repo has no
Python test framework, and adding one to gate content would put half this
plan's evidence in a runner nothing else uses. The generator's contract is its
*output*, so the output is what is asserted over, from the runner already in
use. `py_compile` gates the script's syntax; the rest is checked through the
artifacts.

*Rejected:* one multilingual voice rendering a whole line of mixed narration
in a single call. Simpler, and it puts Thai tone accuracy beyond any check —
CONTEXT.md records the full argument.

*Rejected:* generating audio at request time. Static committed mp3s remove a
runtime dependency and make audio reviewable in a diff.

*Rejected:* caching on the script file's hash rather than per segment. A typo
fix anywhere would re-bill and re-voice the whole lesson, and re-voicing is not
idempotent — the same text returns different audio on a later call.
